themes.name: Materiality
themes.description: Urban surfaces are physical. Every material choice concrete, glass, timber, paint carries embodied energy, a lifespan, and a cultural signal. Materiality asks us to consider what cities are made of, and what those choices mean for durability, identity, and environmental impact over time.

themes.name: Economy
themes.description: The economics of urban surfaces govern who builds, who maintains, and who benefits. From public procurement to private development, financial flows shape what gets built and what decays. Economy examines value beyond cost — the social returns of well-maintained, equitable, and beautiful public surfaces.

themes.name: Governance
themes.description: Who decides what urban surfaces look like? Governance maps the rules, institutions, and authorities that regulate public space. Planning codes, maintenance contracts, and community rights all intersect here. Good governance ensures surfaces reflect collective values rather than narrow interests or bureaucratic inertia.

themes.name: Communication
themes.description: Surfaces speak. Signage, murals, texture, and colour communicate identity, ownership, and invitation. Communication explores how urban surfaces transmit meaning — from wayfinding to political expression — and how communities can reclaim the visual language of their streets and public spaces.

themes.name: Labour
themes.description: Urban surfaces require constant human effort to build, clean, repair, and renew. Labour recognises the workers who sustain our cities — often invisible, often precarious. Valuing their expertise and ensuring fair conditions is central to any serious commitment to high-quality, resilient urban environments.

themes.name: Ecology
themes.description: Every surface is an ecological actor. Pavements affect drainage; green roofs support biodiversity; heat-absorbing materials raise temperatures. Ecology reframes urban surfaces as part of living systems, asking how material choices can support climate resilience, reduce pollution, and make space for non-human life.

nodes.name: Abigail Karas
nodes.relevant focus: Inter-imperial legacies and national identity

nodes.name: Adam Hudec
nodes.relevant focus: Epidermitecture and the organic matter of surface biopatina
nodes.definition: Epidermitecture is concerned with the naturally occurring stains on urban surfaces and is exploring the aesthetic, ecological and functional potential of Urban surfaces within the context of Epidermitecture are defined as living, breathing entities that interact with their environments.

nodes.name: Adrian Burnham
nodes.relevant focus: Oral histories of flyposting in the UK
nodes.definition: A viable surface to an unauthorised commercial fly-poster would be: (i) prominent, visible to passing traffic; (ii) wooden hoardings, shop windows, rendered walls, brickwork; (iii) unlikely to be defaced or torn down; and (iv) not heavily policed.

nodes.name: Adrian Tanner
nodes.relevant focus: Creative graffiti removal practices

nodes.name: Adrienne Cacatian
nodes.relevant focus: Ethnography on propaganda, the aesthetics of authority, and sensory governance

nodes.name: Alex Hale
nodes.relevant focus: Contemporary and historic graffiti and archival surfaces research
nodes.definition: Contemporary urban surfaces are archaeological sites to be considered as feral things. They are rural landscapes tamed by concrete, bricks and mortar. The graffiti are artefacts, previously associated with writing, but now wild; a feraling of sorts. Held within these artefacts are performances of tentacular knowledge networks. Their extent reaches beyond the urban and into a landscape's stratigraphy. As archives they perform a role that disrupts our philosophies, institutions and systems of knowledge-making. As such they are active combinations of archaeological, archival and artefacts.

nodes.name: Alice Mazzilli
nodes.relevant focus: Writing systems, calligraphy, street writing, stylewriting, philosophy of writing
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are relational fields where social, material, environmental, political and technological forces become materially observable. Rather than boundaries between pre-existing entities, they are temporary configurations of relations through which bodies, materials, environments, institutions and technologies continually affect one another, producing shifting forms, meanings, possibilities and ways of experiencing the city.

nodes.name: Alison Barnes
nodes.relevant focus: Urban graphic heritage
nodes.definition: I consider an urban surface as a communicative interface, one that is often inscribed with 'graphic heritage'. Graphic heritage functions as a meaning making system that uses type, colour, symbols and materials.

nodes.name: Andrea Mubi Brighenti
nodes.relevant focus: Publicness, territorology, visibility, sociology of walls
nodes.definition: I like to think of surfaces as convergence space: it's a place where stuff – both material and semiotic – comes and meets from multiple directions. It is a meeting of styles, a clash often. And it surfaces to the extent that it happens in the visible.

nodes.name: Angela (Ange) Glindemann
nodes.relevant focus: Ambient and creative writing

nodes.name: Anne Cronin
nodes.relevant focus: Outdoor advertising, surfaces as calculative spaces, secrecy
nodes.definition: Surfaces are interfaces between processes, practices, institutions and ideas.

nodes.name: Anneke Coppoolse
nodes.relevant focus: Visual communication and everyday aesthetics
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are canvases that reflect current (but also past) conditions (socio-economic, cultural, political) of a place. Though generally vertical and seemingly flat, they are textured, layered, spatial, serving as sites of contestation, scenes of celebration, stages of (and for) interaction, etc.

nodes.name: Anuradha Chatterjee
nodes.relevant focus: Critical architectural theories of the surface as substance

nodes.name: Asees Prab
nodes.relevant focus: Heritage and architectural labour

nodes.name: Ato Jackson
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as educators, images as screens of everyday life

nodes.name: Ayisha Saniya Ambalavan
nodes.relevant focus: Boundary walls and contested heritage
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are constructed architectural layers that shape everyday movement, access and visibility. They act as political agents that divide, segregate and enable violence. Surfaces such as- Walls, fences and borders produce liminal spaces, constantly negotiated and reshaped from below through acts of resistance- graffiti, destruction and acts of crossing.

nodes.name: Billy Potts
nodes.relevant focus: Ghost signs and urban calligraphy

nodes.name: Caroline Kyi
nodes.relevant focus: Critical conservation of outdoor murals

nodes.name: Caroline Millar
nodes.relevant focus: Walking, writing and paying radical attention to the run-off of the streets

nodes.name: Caroline Newton
nodes.relevant focus: Urban democratisation and surface contestation

nodes.name: CC Williams
nodes.relevant focus: Commercial signage and shopfronts

nodes.name: Cecilia Brazioli
nodes.relevant focus: Urban space value, surface evaluation, inscription evaluation
nodes.definition: Within my framework, I deal with Urban Surfaces both as canvases for the expression of conflicting instances, and as penetrable boundaries that allow for the visibilisation of ongoing negotiations on the aesthetic and visual order of contemporary cities.

nodes.name: Cheng Chen
nodes.relevant focus: LED urbanism and nighttime surface displays

nodes.name: Chris Boyko
nodes.relevant focus: Pavement surfaces and stayability
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces, in the form of pavements (or sidewalks, footpaths etc.), refer to any publicly negotiated horizontal planes, from carriageway edge to other thresholds (e.g., buildings, green spaces), on which legal rights, social meanings and economic values are inscribed and may be contested.

nodes.name: Chris Parkinson
nodes.relevant focus: Collective art practices and street posters
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are a portal into sinewy networks of rhythmic, relational and nonrepresentational concepts of urban space.

nodes.name: Christoph Lueder
nodes.relevant focus: Material transformation, architectural divides between public/ private
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are interfaces between a material condition and transformative forces. Urban surfaces result from claims to space and often have an invisible interior counterpart. As urban laboratories such surfaces record entangled processes between urban and interior milieus and constitute living archives of material-social processes and individuation.

nodes.name: Cristian Simonetti
nodes.relevant focus: Anthropology of surfaces, gestures, and time
nodes.definition: Surfaces are where action and history entangle and endure.

nodes.name: Dan Johnston
nodes.relevant focus: Skateboarding and skatepark surface traces
nodes.definition: In my research, urban surfaces encompass all skatepark elements—concrete, steel, timber structures, signage, boundary zones, and surrounding trees. These surfaces serve dual functions: providing physical skating terrain and operating as canvases where users inscribe cultural traces.

nodes.name: David Littlefield
nodes.relevant focus: Urban legibility and reading of surfaces

nodes.name: David Pontille
nodes.relevant focus: Surface maintenance and orderings, graffiti removal, urban inscriptions
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces raise at least three challenges. Instead of being already there, they are the outcome of an uncertain materialization process. They are technically enacted as sites of particular material politics. And they are unruly, fragile entities calling for constant care.

nodes.name: Diana-Raisa Lolici
nodes.relevant focus: Street art culture
nodes.definition: I conceptualise urban surfaces as both material supports and socio-political interfaces that mediate artistic expression, control, and public engagement. Far from neutral, urban surfaces embody layered histories and meanings, functioning as contested sites where authority and resistance converge.

nodes.name: Diandra Saginatari
nodes.relevant focus: Architectural porosity and surface ecology of heritage façades
nodes.definition: Urban surface, exemplified by walls and façades, is a contested porous boundary exposed to the public realm. Its varying degrees of material, spatial and social porosity allow the emergence of socio-spatial, socio-political, cultural and ecological thickness, mediating formal and informal appropriation, communication, interpretation and inhabitation by human and non-human actors.

nodes.name: Dina Yunis
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as political palimpsests; graffiti and dissent in conflict cities
nodes.definition: In conflict cities like Beirut, the publicly visible urban surface is a politically charged interface and a contested palimpsest. Its functions are threefold: as a chronicle of dissent, a nexus of power reclaiming space, and a site of contested memory archiving alternative histories.

nodes.name: Doron Altaratz
nodes.relevant focus: Computational imaging of heritage surfaces as embodied interfaces

nodes.name: Eduardo de la Fuente
nodes.relevant focus: Texturology and the skin of the city
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are the plethora of built and natural things that provide cities, regions, and places with distinctive surficial qualities, and I am very interested in the kinds of metaphors that also get generated to talk about surfaces. I'm authoring something in Spanish at the moment called La piel de la ciudad, The skin of the city. There are interesting feminist writings about buildings and cities being clothed, or dressed, faces and interfaces.

nodes.name: Efrîn Özyetiş
nodes.relevant focus: Facades and digital renditions

nodes.name: Elijah Agwaru Anomet
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti art for community and the environment
nodes.definition: Urban Surfaces are constantly evolving interfaces that intersect the material environment and culture, encompassing, but not limited to, rhythms, structures, textures, and spaces, that serve as canvases for community perspectives.

nodes.name: Eliza Demian Patrascu
nodes.relevant focus: Dereliction, decay, and surface textures

nodes.name: Emina Zejnilović
nodes.relevant focus: Architectural surfaces and walking methods
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are not passive backdrops, they are the city's quiet witnesses, recording its transformations in cracks, textures, and layers of paint and mortar. They are the visual soundtracks of political shifts, social currents, and cultural memory.

nodes.name: Emma McRae
nodes.relevant focus: Urban imaginaries and digital representation

nodes.name: Enzo Lara-Hamilton
nodes.relevant focus: Urban mythology through street-art

nodes.name: Erna Husukic
nodes.relevant focus: Architectural surfaces and walking methods
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are not passive backdrops, they are the city's quiet witnesses, recording its transformations in cracks, textures, and layers of paint and mortar. They are the visual soundtracks of political shifts, social currents, and cultural memory.

nodes.name: Esther Kiruba Jebakumar Clifford
nodes.relevant focus: Murals as community assets

nodes.name: Eynat Mendelson-Shwartz
nodes.relevant focus: Mural and street art policies

nodes.name: Francesca Bragaglia
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti slogans and urban power

nodes.name: Frederico Câmara
nodes.relevant focus: Documentation of hand painted commercial signage

nodes.name: Friederike Landau-Donnelly
nodes.relevant focus: Political difference of public art via administrative 'politics' and self-inscribed mo(ve)ments of 'the political'
nodes.definition: As an interdisciplinary spatial theorist and cultural geographer, I approach urban surfaces as contested socio-spatial arrangements. Surfaces are mediated by human and more-than-human actors as material-symbolical matter, materialising in different constellations of property, power and place... Surfaces are palimpsests.

nodes.name: Gabriel Araújo Velasco
nodes.relevant focus: Pichação and historiographies of inscriptions

nodes.name: Gerda Wielander
nodes.relevant focus: Visual communication, cultural history
nodes.definition: Walls are remnant traces of traditional and socialist urban structures that serve as loci of memory and as medium to host ever new traces in the form of writing, painting, spraying, and printing by a variety of actors, including the state. They are documents forming a fragile archive providing insights into how society works and feels.

nodes.name: Greg Ireland
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti removal chemicals and training

nodes.name: Hans Leo Maes
nodes.relevant focus: Buff photography and surface traces

nodes.name: Heather Shirey
nodes.relevant focus: Race and identity in murals and street art

nodes.name: Holly Carton
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces of conflict, memorialisation and the Belfast Peace Walls

nodes.name: Iain White
nodes.relevant focus: Mural festival commissioning and curation
nodes.definition: I see a surface as a small part of a wider urban story. Surfaces provide visual cues into the condition of a city and its inhabitants, from the movements of capital, to its politics or population diversity, to its relationship with nature or risk.

nodes.name: Ingrid Halland
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces in art and architecture; history of titanium white and whiteness in modernism
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces serve as aesthetic contact zones between man-made materials, individual experiences, and global meaning-making, including politics, ethics, and cultural values.

nodes.name: Jack Wu
nodes.relevant focus: Human-centred design and public space activation

nodes.name: Jacob Kimvall
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti as text and surfaces as intertextual spaces
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are texts, and graffiti is thus text upon text.

nodes.name: Jane Elizabeth Bennett
nodes.relevant focus: Pavement surfaces as perceived by autistic women
nodes.definition: I am defining the urban floorscape as a locomotable surface; a dynamic interface between body and environment that supports walking and mobility-aid use. Carrying traces of history and everyday rhythms, it entangles movement with embodied knowledge.

nodes.name: Jazoo Yang
nodes.relevant focus: Murals and creative practices of urban memory
nodes.definition: In my practice, urban surfaces function as tactile archives where materials, memory, and human contact converge. They record traces of lived experience and transformation.

nodes.name: JC Viloria
nodes.relevant focus: Aesthetic strategies of urban governance and regulation

nodes.name: Jenny Papasotiriou
nodes.relevant focus: Heritage education and decolonial spatial justice
nodes.definition: Curvey, flat, stepped on, wheeled on, looked up to, prominent or hidden surfaces that serve as canvas for silenced (hi)stories and silenced city dwellers across generations colonising the public sphere, while producing, exchanging and disseminating decolonial knowledge.

nodes.name: Jessica Amarteifio
nodes.relevant focus: Indigenous knowledges in urban surface governance
nodes.definition: Urban Surfaces are the maintained living skins of public spaces. Spaces keep evolving, just like humans. This means, the definition of surfaces in urban areas is dynamic, with regards to walkways, walls and overheads. With this in view, sustainable urban surfaces require locally sourced materials, for urban continuity and to reduce environmental harm.

nodes.name: Joanne Choueiri
nodes.relevant focus: Construction hoardings and wish images
nodes.definition: In my work, urban surfaces are exemplified by the construction fence: a surface that hides a demolition, a construction, or a stalled reconstruction while displaying Walter Benjamin's idea of 'wish images'. These curated visuals project developer, state, and civic futures, making the fence an active political interface rather than a neutral barrier.

nodes.name: Joumana Ibrahim
nodes.relevant focus: Vernacular visuals and urban marks in post-conflict cities
nodes.definition: In conflict and post-conflict cities, a surface is never neutral. It becomes a canvas, a pattern, a banner. It is a call for action, a gesture of resilience, a cry for help, and a threat that marks territory. It can be an invitation, a sacred space, or a battlefield of meaning. In cities caught in conflicts and their aftermath, surfaces speak for both the oppressed and the oppressors.

nodes.name: Juan Carlos Guerrero-Hernandez
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as cultural interfaces and sites of memory

nodes.name: Julia Tulke
nodes.relevant focus: Aesthetics of crisis and longitudinal documentation of surfaces
nodes.definition: Surfaces are historically accumulated materialities that can be activated or deactivated by performative intervention or the strategic prevention thereof, often in counterintuitive ways.

nodes.name: Kathryn Ewing
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as social (co-)infrastructures of memory and community

nodes.name: Katya Assaf Zakharov
nodes.relevant focus: Legal reimaginings of public walls
nodes.definition: For us, urban surfaces are sites of semiotic control and resistance. Urban surfaces tell us stories of wealth and poverty, of power and weakness, of social acceptance and rejection, of winners and losers. For instance, billboards indoctrinate the hegemony of consumer culture in our society; whitewashed graffiti signifies that personal messages are a suppressed dissent in the semiotics of public space.

nodes.name: Kel Glaister
nodes.relevant focus: Parkour and the visibility of playability

nodes.name: Kevin Muldoon-Smith
nodes.relevant focus: Pavement surfaces and stayability
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces, in the form of pavements (or sidewalks, footpaths etc.), refer to any publicly negotiated horizontal planes, from carriageway edge to other thresholds (e.g., buildings, green spaces), on which legal rights, social meanings and economic values are inscribed and may be contested.

nodes.name: Konstantinos Avramidis
nodes.relevant focus: Drawing, tracing and mapping traces of inhabitation; graffiti writing and removal
nodes.definition: Urban Surfaces are material graphic archives where inhabitation—and, therefore, contestation—is inscribed. Surfaces are multivocal, multitemporal structures where, often opposing, agents meet to express opinions, exercise rights and negotiate power.

nodes.name: Krystal Kehoe
nodes.relevant focus: Social media use by graffiti writers

nodes.name: Kurt Iveson
nodes.relevant focus: Spatial justice, public space
nodes.definition: Surfaces are contested street media, which dramatise an inescapable tension between authorisation and appropriation in public spaces, in capitalist cities.

nodes.name: Kyle Magee
nodes.relevant focus: Democratisation of advertising and media sites

nodes.name: Laura Szyman
nodes.relevant focus: Illustration-led approaces to market-driven housing

nodes.name: Lesley Pleasant
nodes.relevant focus: Filmic representations of city surfaces, library surfaces

nodes.name: Linda Matthews
nodes.relevant focus: Visualisation technologies and urban surveillance

nodes.name: Liz Oakley-Brown
nodes.relevant focus: Transhistorical textual study of surfaces
nodes.definition: In 2017, Rebecca Coleman and I argued that 'The surface is …potentially manifold and politically contingent' (2017: 6). By taking up and developing our earlier point, I define urban surfaces as parts of the physical environment dependent on scale, semiotics and social justice i.e. what's visible, what's communicable, and who matters?

nodes.name: Lorenzo "SERRAGLIA” Servi
nodes.relevant focus: Accidental monuments, urban photography
nodes.definition: For me, urban surfaces are like diaries, or even ancient tablets. They record both voluntary and involuntary actions: scratches, stains, repairs, graffiti, weather. In my practice, I treat them as signs to be translated into a visual language, so their hidden meanings become visible to everyone.

nodes.name: Lucy Finchett-Maddock
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti, property, the commons, theories of art/law
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are legal etchings upon which the cityscape writes. They are rich tapestries of spatial code. They are the edge of law. And they are law.

nodes.name: Lucy Irvine
nodes.relevant focus: Textiles as design, urban public sculpture
nodes.definition: I consider an urban surface as a boundary or an interface. My expanded textile practice involves generating new urban surfaces that intervene in public space. By weaving unpredictable emergent forms from materials that usually play a utilitarian homogenising role in the urban fabric, I seek to confuse boundaries and open new interfaces.

nodes.name: Maggie Kusenbach
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti and street art festivals, urban development, ethnography
nodes.definition: From my viewpoint as an urban sociologist, urban surfaces are places in the public realm, a social territory dominated by strangers and governed by implicit rules for interaction and relationships... material and symbolic props citizens can use to express and manage identities.

nodes.name: Marguerite Coetzee
nodes.relevant focus: Ethnographies of spatial futures, foregrounding various states of matter
nodes.definition: The urban surface is a layered, palimpsestic register, the concrete, upper crust through which the urban fabric becomes legible. It is simultaneously a spatial archive, holding traces of what the city has been, and a spatial proposition, of what could be. It is always under construction, always emergent, always coming undone.

nodes.name: Maria Chatzidakis
nodes.relevant focus: materials, restoration, street art heritage
nodes.definition: From a conservator's perspective, urban surfaces can be seen as the physical structures, the skin, the outer layer of the urban environment, the interface of the city as a living monument. It is a palimpsest of layered history, that forms the intricate fabric of a city, both visible and hidden.

nodes.name: Megan Hicks
nodes.relevant focus: Pavement surfaces, the urban horizontal
nodes.definition: In my work I concentrate on horizontal urban surfaces, or pavements. By 'pavements' I mean paved public spaces, including roadways, footpaths, sidewalks and public squares. I approach this subject in two ways... I have found that the pavement is more than a passive platform for feet and wheels. Rather, it is both a canvas for written expression and a presence in its own right, contributing to the conscious and subconscious cultural life of a city.

nodes.name: Melissa Smith
nodes.relevant focus: Boundary walls, territories

nodes.name: Meng Hsuan-Lee
nodes.relevant focus: Façades, screens, signage

nodes.name: Mia Gaia Trentin
nodes.relevant focus: Historic graffiti, documentation
nodes.definition: The surface is an interactive space that collects a wide variety of anthropic marks of interaction, performed with different intentions for different reasons through different media. In this sense, the surface becomes a repository of collective memory, meanings, and values for the communities experiencing the place.

nodes.name: Michael Stonham
nodes.relevant focus: The fifth elevation in 3D design, graffiti in/and interior architecture

nodes.name: Mirame Elsayed
nodes.relevant focus: Psychologies of the urban surface

nodes.name: Miti Kinaawola
nodes.relevant focus: Everyday life of urban surfaces, urban tours, informal writing practices
nodes.definition: Through my practice as a tour guide at Tembea Kampala Walking Tours, urban surfaces are the visible and tangible layers through which the city's social, cultural, and political life is recorded and made legible... In my work, urban surfaces are texts to be read and stories to be experienced.

nodes.name: Moral Masuoka
nodes.relevant focus: Socially-engaged mural production, socially-sustainable mural production
nodes.definition: Within my work producing murals, I define an urban surface as a solid structure, typically a wall, to which paint can be applied, that provides visual experiences within the environment.

nodes.name: Myrto Tsilimpounidi
nodes.relevant focus: Photography, feminist and queer approaches to street politics
nodes.definition: I have always been interested in the surfacing concerns and political tensions on the urban surfaces as evident below.

nodes.name: Natalie Bauer
nodes.relevant focus: Stickers as an artistic and communicative device
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces consist of street furniture, like walls or lampposts, that make public space a room. In combination with Henri Lefebvre's reflections on the visual expression of power dynamics in cities, furniture decorated with street art makes the room a home for its inhabitants. Consequently, urban surfaces constitute the canvas upon which the public can express their ideas and engage with each other.

nodes.name: Nataly Arevalo
nodes.relevant focus: Municipal perspectives on surface management

nodes.name: Nazanin
nodes.relevant focus: Feminist approaches, representation and protest in murals

nodes.name: Nian Paul
nodes.relevant focus: Feminist approaches to urban visual governance and spatial justice
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are material configurations of socio-spatial relations, political expressions, contestations, resilience and future imaginaries. I position public art as not just an adornment on urban surfaces, but an urban surface itself.

nodes.name: Nina O’Reilly
nodes.relevant focus: Resistance to neoliberal urban regeneration and development

nodes.name: Panos Leventis
nodes.relevant focus: Street art in/and narratives of the urban
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are immersive sites of experience, from where two-dimensional space expands, fusing built fabric with creative forces and active publics, retelling the city to the city.

nodes.name: Pati Starzykowski
nodes.relevant focus: Political agency of abjectified urban ecologies as knowledge producers
nodes.definition: A living, breathing, acting child of many, born out of necessity but grown and growing into its own capacity to tell stories of where it came from, what it endured, what was lost, what was gained, what still holds, and what holds what.

nodes.name: Peta Carlin
nodes.relevant focus: Movements between surfaces, including architectural, textile & photographic
nodes.definition: In my photographic series, Urban Fabric, the commonplace textile metaphor was engaged... The significance of the image as a surface, for my practice, is its capacity to mediate and establish dialogues between different places, cultures and disciplines.

nodes.name: Peter Bengtsen
nodes.relevant focus: (Unsanctioned) expressions and the publicness of public space; street art and democracy
nodes.definition: I do not believe it is necessary, or possible, to come up with a single definition of the urban surface. However, for me, urban surfaces often function as waymarkers. Along a particular path, or street, remembering street names is much less helpful for navigating the urban environment than recognising urban surfaces.

nodes.name: Petr Vašát
nodes.relevant focus: Macromurals
nodes.definition: Drawing on the case of macromurals, urban surfaces are a heterogeneous, uneven ensemble of material planes—walls, façades, roofs—and other built or natural textures that become temporarily homogenised through painting, maintenance, or infrastructural intervention into cohesive visual patterns visible from a great distance.

nodes.name: Phoebe Whitman
nodes.relevant focus: Interiority and materiality of surfaces, practices of surface care

nodes.name: Pierre-Edourad Weill
nodes.relevant focus: Governance of graffiti, advertising and the attention economy
nodes.definition: Through my sociological research, I conceptualise urban surfaces as public or private supports for graffiti and street art. I analyse their legal framing, exploring how penalisation intersects with artistic legitimation via court cases, specialised policing, and digital surveillance, while examining how symbolic capital circulates and converts into economic value.

nodes.name: Preeti Mudliar
nodes.relevant focus: Autorickshaw screens as mobile archives of film fandom in traffic

nodes.name: Rafael Schacter
nodes.relevant focus: Public art, graffiti, and urban visual cultures
nodes.definition: Urban seems easy enough define - something of or related to the city - whilst surfaces presents us with both a physical and conceptual idea of a boundary point (often between inside and out, above and below). In this context, however, and in today's increasingly surveilled, securitised, and privatised megalopolises, 'urban surfaces' are critical spaces of conflict and contestation revealing the messy complexity of the city today.

nodes.name: Rainier Leloup
nodes.relevant focus: Graffiti

nodes.name: Richard Müller
nodes.relevant focus: Compound walls in India and Taiwan
nodes.definition: Any attempt to produce a definition of an urban surface must anticipate its role in the shaping, configuration, and mediation of social dynamics within the city it is situated. Urban surfaces exceed their status as palimpsests by possessing the capacity to intervene in the socio-urban spaces of cities.

nodes.name: Robert Harland
nodes.relevant focus: Urban graphic heritage

nodes.name: Ronald Kramer
nodes.relevant focus: Street art, graffiti, state intervention in public space
nodes.definition: I find it incredibly difficult to provide a definition of urban surfaces... an urban surface is a feature of the urban environment that people have some meaningful, democratic claim to; those parts of the city that the people build and support.

nodes.name: Ruth Dalton
nodes.relevant focus: Pavement surfaces and stayability
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces, in the form of pavements (or sidewalks, footpaths etc.), refer to any publicly negotiated horizontal planes, from carriageway edge to other thresholds (e.g., buildings, green spaces), on which legal rights, social meanings and economic values are inscribed and may be contested.

nodes.name: Sabina Andron
nodes.relevant focus: Urban visual governance, graffiti removal and public images
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are contested semiotic territories of spatial co-production and public address. I am interested in how surfaces create meaning and how signage positions this meaning, as well as how surfaces are regulated.

nodes.name: Samuel Holleran
nodes.relevant focus: Community input and management of memorials, urban parks, and public spaces
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are planes, normally parallel to a viewer's gaze. They remain visible over time but take on new textures and skins. Surfaces are mostly constructed, but natural elements can be altered to become surfaces. An urban tree trunk or rock wall isn’t a surface until it’s painted or posted on.

nodes.name: Selma Piukovici
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as infrastructures of publicness

nodes.name: Serhat Ay
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as public infrastructures under authoritarian urbanism

nodes.name: Shruti Mehta
nodes.relevant focus: Public art as regenerative strategy

nodes.name: Simon Marvin
nodes.relevant focus: Surfaces as climate technologies and infrastructures
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces - building walls and roofs, ground space including hard landscaping, water features and green nature - are being actively reconfigured as climate technologies to strategically modulate energy, thermal, liquid and chemical flows at the interface of atmospheric and terrestrial milieus.

nodes.name: Siri Haavimb
nodes.relevant focus: Ambiguities of disorder

nodes.name: Sneha Annavarapu
nodes.relevant focus: Road surfaces, potholes and driving in India
nodes.definition: Surfaces are the skin of the roads that motorists drive on. I approach the surface not as an object but as the sensation felt by motoring bodies as they move on roads.

nodes.name: Soufiane Chinig
nodes.relevant focus:
An ethnography of graffiti writing, festival-based mural painting and cultural
diplomacy.
nodes.definition: In my work on Jordan and Morocco, urban surfaces materialise as pages where actors write, draw, paint and design their social and political worlds. The state, artists and anonymous writers of different ages, genders, and walks of life create and use surfaces to channel ideologies, circulate meanings and (re)define subjectivities.

nodes.name: Sprya Sharma
nodes.relevant focus: Socio-political semiotics of walls
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces act as display boards where the needs of the governed and the interests of government intersect, offering insights into societal structures and issues. The surfaces not only reflect the society they also sustain the society.

nodes.name: Susan Hansen
nodes.relevant focus: Documentation and reception of graffiti and street art
nodes.definition: I document walls over time as urban social surfaces, in order to make available for analysis the ongoing collective dialogue on city walls, taking into account not just monumental murals and subcultural graffiti but the entire spectrum of quotidian urban inscriptions.

nodes.name: Susanna Newbury
nodes.relevant focus: Art and architecture in real estate and economics
nodes.definition: Surfaces are long-standing symptoms of the consequences of past intervention.

nodes.name: Svetlana Feokistova
nodes.relevant focus: Documentation of buffing and urban walls

nodes.name: Tara Di Cassio
nodes.relevant focus: Material cultural worlds on walls across fragmented geographies
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are vulnerable and everchanging spaces. Though urban planning and architecture schemes attempt to fix them, they are already vulnerable to intervention and decay at the moment of their installation. Surfaces and their inherent vulnerability make them continuous sites of (re)activation, (re)constitution, and (re)purposing by human and non-human forces.

nodes.name: Taylor Coyne
nodes.relevant focus: Urban water ecologies and hydrosurfaces
nodes.definition: In my work as a historical and political urban geographer of stormwater infrastructures, I define urban surfaces through the lens of infrastructure, drains, and urban swamps. They are porous, layered skins through which water, memory, and power move. A surface is not a boundary but a threshold: archive, ecology, and territory.

nodes.name: Tim Ingold
nodes.relevant focus: Anthropology of lines, surfaces, materiality
nodes.definition: By the urban surface, I refer to the ground of what is commonly called the 'built environment'. It is distinguished by being paved.

nodes.name: Tim Schnetgöke
nodes.relevant focus: Billboards and public walls
nodes.definition: For us, urban surfaces are sites of semiotic control and resistance. Urban surfaces tell us stories of wealth and poverty, of power and weakness, of social acceptance and rejection, of winners and losers. For instance, billboards indoctrinate the hegemony of consumer culture in our society; whitewashed graffiti signifies that personal messages are a suppressed dissent in the semiotics of public space.

nodes.name: Tom Critchley
nodes.relevant focus: E-transport infrastructure, skateboarding, graffiti
nodes.definition: An urban surface is where city materialities and social practices interact, overlap, and are (re)configured. As a designer, I do not see them as passive backdrops, but active canvases to express and understand identity, culture, and socialities of the city, alongside a space to intervene and reconfigure these relationships. In the context of my research on micromobility, urban surfaces are the public facing representations of transport infrastructure: pavements, curbs, cycle lanes, docking zones, and e-bikes/e-scooters themselves.

nodes.name: Tom Ward
nodes.relevant focus: Hand-painted advertising, mural labour, surface commodification
nodes.definition: Urban surfaces are the nexus at which vertical space and public space intersect; they are where material infrastructures gain agency by being activated as public, as visible, as sites of contestation.

nodes.definition: Archived urban imageries are also urban surfaces. Every storefront, advertisement and graffiti exists not only as a physical surface on walls but as explorable data within Google Street View's archive, a digital twin of cities for the past 18 years.
